items.title: Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts general availability
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts is now generally available. It remediates alerts by working across your codebase the way a developer would: it explores relevant files, proposes a fix, and reruns CodeQL to confirm the fix closes the alert before opening a pull request for your review. Agentic autofix is available to GitHub Code Security and GitHub Advanced Security customers on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. How it works When you assign a code scanning alert to Copilot, it: Explores relevant files across your codebase. Generates a proposed fix. Validates the fix works by rerunning CodeQL. Iterates if needed, then opens a draft pull request ready for your review. The pull request includes a summary of the fix, why it closes the alert, and the validation steps Copilot took to confirm that it works. When the pull request containing the fix is ready, you can instruct Copilot to make further changes to it by commenting on the pull request or interacting with the session in the Agents tab of your repository. How to use it When enabled, agentic autofix replaces the free Generate Fix option on individual code scanning alerts with an Assign to Copilot button. You can use agentic autofix: From any code scanning alert on the repository’s default branch, by assigning the alert to Copilot. In the list of security alerts in your repository or security campaign, by selecting up to 25 alerts for Copilot to fix together in a single pull request. Via the Update a Code Scanning Alert REST API by setting assignees to ["copilot-swe-agent[bot]"]. Agentic autofix supports code scanning alerts on the repository’s default branch. Alerts detected only on pull requests or other branches cannot be assigned to Copilot. Access Agentic autofix requires an enterprise administrator to enable access to it via the new “Agentic autofix” policy in Advanced Security policies. items.title: AI Scan for pull requests generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Code scanning AI Scan for pull requests is now generally available. It complements CodeQL by finding vulnerabilities in pull request changes for languages and frameworks that CodeQL does not currently cover, including PHP, Shell/Bash, Terraform configuration (HCL), Dockerfiles, JSP for Java, Blazor for C#, and more. How it works AI Scan runs automatically on pull requests when code scanning and the repository’s effective AI Scan setting are enabled. Findings appear alongside CodeQL results on the Conversation and Files changed tabs, with an “AI” indicator to distinguish them from CodeQL alerts. Findings can include an explanation of the security risk and a suggested autofix. AI Scan findings are advisory. They do not fail the code scanning check and cannot block pull request merges through ruleset requirements. AI Scan does not run on pull requests from forks or pull requests created by Dependabot. Availability AI Scan is available for public repositories owned by organizations or personal accounts. For private and internal organization-owned repositories, GitHub Code Security or GitHub Advanced Security is required. A GitHub Copilot license is not required. Billing AI Scan for pull requests consumes Code Security AI Credits. AI Credit usage is displayed in the “AI usage” section of enterprise billing and licensing as the “Advanced Security” product. You can also set SKU-level budgets for Code Security AI Credits. Learn more about usage-based billing. Learn more about AI Scan for pull requests and billing for GitHub Advanced Security AI features. Join the discussion in the AI Scan Community discussion. The post AI Scan for pull requests generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: GitHub AI Scan is now GA and covers Dockerfiles, Terraform and Shell in PRs beyond CodeQL. It could add a useful security gate to client CI review pipelines.

items.title: Download GitHub Code Quality license usage as a CSV
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now download a CSV report of your GitHub Code Quality license usage to reconcile your license count with your own records. The report includes: Each active committer who consumes a Code Quality license. The repositories that received their commits in the last 90 days. Whether each committer is unique to a single repository or organization. Use the unique committer details to identify where disabling Code Quality could free up licenses for the next billing period without changing your current license charge. To download your report, go to the Billing and licensing page in your organization or enterprise, open Licensing, and download the CSV from the Code Quality card. CSV downloads are available on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud. For details, see Viewing and managing GitHub Code Quality costs. Join the discussion in GitHub Community. items.title: Email notifications for repository push events have been retired
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: As of October 15, 2026, email notifications for repository push events have been retired and are no longer sent. We shut down this feature to help prevent spam and abuse. Because recipients didn’t have to consent before receiving these emails, the feature could be misused to send unwanted messages through GitHub’s email infrastructure. To continue sending email notifications for repository push events, you can use a GitHub Actions workflow triggered by push events to send emails through your own SMTP server or email provider. The post Email notifications for repository push events have been retired appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: GitHub has retired push event email notifications. This is a minor change, and any team that relies on them can rebuild it with a GitHub Actions workflow.

items.title: v2.1.301
items.author: ashwin-ant
items.excerpt: What's changed Added CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS so unattended retry mode (CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG) ends a request at a usage limit that resets too far away instead of waiting Added OpenTelemetry tracing guidance to the claude-api skill, including setting up trace destinations with the ant CLI Added the % motion to vim mode: jump to the matching bracket, alone or with d/c/y Added rows to a mod's Input: a text field of several lines in the terminal, where Enter submits and Shift+Enter or a backslash before Enter starts a new line Added classifier_verdict and permission_mode to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, so auto mode classifier decisions can be told apart from permission rules Added classifier_category to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, naming the built-in rule a classifier block matched, when OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 Fixed quitting removing a worktree made by a WorktreeCreate hook without asking when it may hold unpushed commits Fixed the fable (and best) model alias erroring on the Anthropic API when the newest Fable model is not available to your organization: Claude Code now retries once on the previous Fable model Fixed a misleading "Please run /login" error when a full disk keeps the login from being refreshed; the error now names the disk and says to delete files Fixed Grep and Glob reporting no matches when the search program failed unexpectedly before returning any results; they now return an error saying the search failed Fixed workflow agents sometimes skipping their step, and the run still reporting success, after reading the harness note that their task text carries no user authority Fixed artifact updates being refused where a PreToolUse hook covers Edit or Write; Claude now edits the file and then republishes instead of changing it in the publish call Fixed skills and commands with very many or very long argument names stalling for seconds when invoked; only the first 64 names, each up to 64 characters, are now fill
items.why_it_matters: Claude Code v2.1.301 adds a retry watchdog usage-limit cap for unattended runs, OpenTelemetry guidance and permission classifier fields. It directly affects agent pipelines.

items.title: Tree Appreciator
items.excerpt: Tool: Tree Appreciator Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk, I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play. Tags: game-design, javascript, ai, generative-ai, llms, claude, vibe-coding, three-js

items.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
items.excerpt: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from "people with knowledge of the matter". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" (previously) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic
items.why_it_matters: Anthropic's revenue grew fast ahead of its IPO, which signals that Claude vendor demand is stable. It is market context for advising clients and has no direct engineering impact.
